```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(emmeans)
library(broom)
```



## Reminder: Linear Model Assumptions


- In every model (discussed so far), we assume the experimental error is: $\epsilon \overset{iid}{\sim} N(0, \sigma^2)$

- In other words, the errors are: 
  - **Independent** (iid)
  - **Normal** ($\sim$ N(,))
  - & have **Equal Variance** ($\sigma^2$)

## Reminder: Checking Linear Model Assumptions

  - **Independence**: based on context...  
  - **Normality**: QQplot of residuals
  - **Equal Variance**: Scatter plot of residuals vs. predicted values
  

## What to do if our assumptions are broken...

Big picture:

:::callout-important
### Not Independent

There is nothing that you can do at the analysis stage for this... make sure that you have independent experimental units through your design!
:::

:::columns

:::column

:::callout-warning
### Non-constant Residual Variance

1. Welch's ANOVA
2. Try transforming the outcomes ($y$'s)
3. Generalized Linear Models (GLMs)

:::
:::

:::column

:::callout-warning
### Non-normality of Residuals

1. Try transforming the outcomes ($y$'s)
2. Non-parametric tests
3. Bootstrap simulation

:::
:::
:::
  
Details to come...

# Unequal Variance

## Example -- unequal variance

- Suppose we apply three treatments (A, B, and C) to 10 experimental units each (total n = N = 30) and measure a response, $y_{ij}$. 
- If the variance differs across treatments, our standard ANOVA may not be appropriate.

:::columns

:::column
```{r}
set.seed(34)

a <- rnorm(10, mean = 4, sd = 1)
b <- rnorm(10, mean = 10, sd = 4)
c <- rnorm(10, mean = 8, sd = 4)

unvar_dat <- tibble(subj. = 1:30,
                    treat = rep(c("A","B","C"), each = 10),
                    y = c(a,b,c))

unvar_dat |> 
  group_by(treat) |> 
  summarize(mean_resp = mean(y),
            sd_resp = sd(y)) |>  
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)

```
:::
:::column
```{r}

unvar_dat |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = treat, y = y)) + 
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_jitter(height = 0) +
  labs(x = "treatment")
```
:::
:::


## Example -- unequal variance - ANOVA


::::columns

:::column

:::callout-warning
# Incorrect Analysis 

```{r}
#| echo: true

options(contrasts = c("contr.sum", "contr.poly"))

bad_mod <- lm(y ~ treat, data = unvar_dat)

anova(bad_mod)
```
```{r}
#| echo: true

emmeans(bad_mod, specs = ~treat)
```
:::
:::


:::column

:::callout-warning
# Uh-Oh!
```{r}
bad_mod |> 
  broom::augment() |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = .fitted, y = .resid)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0,
             color = "#3a86d4") +
  labs(x = "Fitted Values", y = "Residuals")
```

:::
:::
::::

## Formal Test(s) for Unequal Variance

$$H_0: \sigma_A = \sigma_B = \sigma_C$$
$$H_A: \text{At least one } \sigma_i \text{ is different.}$$

```{r}
#| echo: true

bartlett.test(y ~ treat, data = unvar_dat)
```
```{r}
#| echo: true

car::leveneTest(y ~ treat, data = unvar_dat)
```


## Welch's ANOVA


```{r}
#| echo: true

welch_test <- oneway.test(y ~ treat, data = unvar_dat)

welch_test
```



## Welch's ANOVA -- follow-up analyses {.scrollable}

:::columns
:::{.column width=47.5%}

```{r}
#| echo: true

t.test(y ~ treat, 
       data = unvar_dat |> filter(treat %in% c("A","B")),
       var.equal = F)
```

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| 
t.test(y ~ treat, 
       data = unvar_dat |> filter(treat %in% c("C","B")),
       var.equal = F)
```
:::

:::{.column width=5%}

:::

:::{.column width=47.5%}

:::callout-tip

Follow-up analyses done "by hand" with all pairwise t-test  **assuming unequal variance**, then **apply Bonferroni adjustment** "by hand"

:::
```{r}
#| echo: true
#| 
t.test(y ~ treat, 
       data = unvar_dat |> filter(treat %in% c("A","C")),
       var.equal = F)
```



:::

:::

## Generalized Linear Models (GLM)

- If the response variable is **not** **continuous** (think counts or a binary 1/0 (yes/no)), then there may be unequal variation between groups.
- If the sample size is big enough, you may be okay on normality, but not on equal variation.
- One approach to this is using a GLM that is appropriate for that type of response
  - Poisson (count response)
  - Logistic (binary response)


# Non-Normality

## Assessing Non-Normality

::: callout-tip

## CLT is friend

Especially when sample sizes are relatively large, we usually don't have to worry too much about whether the response variable is normally distributed
:::

- Check normality with QQ-plot
- If normality is just a little off, try applying a log or square root transormation to the response (y)
- If normality appears to be **severely violated,** use non-parametric tests




## Non-Parametric Tests

- Non-parametric tests don't make assumptions about the distribution of the errors (and responses!)
- Take advantage of randomization for inference
- They are typically **robust** to skew and outliers
- Less powerful than ANOVA if ANOVA assumptions actually hold



## Kruskal-Wallis / Wilcoxon Rank-Sum / Mann-Whitney U Test (CRD)

$$H_0: \text{There is no true effect of the treatment on the response}$$

$$H_A: \text{There is a true effect of the treatment on the response}$$

**Big picture**: Create a test statistic based on the **ranks** of the responses that compares the treatment groups


<br>


:::callout-note
### Why all the names?

The Kruskal-Wallis test is an extension of the Wilcoxon Rank-Sum (or Mann-Whitney U) test, to accommodate more than two treatment groups. Wilcoxon and Mann & Whitney just came up with the same test independently at the same time (1945-47)!

:::

## Kruskal-Wallis Test - Example 

:::columns

:::{.column width=55%}


**Example:** We got 48 friends to test what griddle temperature (levels 4 or 6) and time on the griddle (2 or 3 minutes) makes the best pancakes! You have each friend eat one short stack of pancakes made on the same griddle, with 2 oz of batter each and 1 oz of maple syrup on top. They rate the pancakes from 1-10 (10 is the best).


```{r}
set.seed(03)

pancakes <- readxl::read_xlsx("_data/07-pancakes.xlsx") |> 
  mutate(rating = rating + sample(0:5)) |> 
  mutate(treatment = str_c(temperature, " & ", time))

pancakes |> 
  dplyr::select(temperature, time, rating, treatment) |> 
  knitr::kable() |> 
    kableExtra::scroll_box(height = "200px") |> 
  kableExtra::kable_styling(font_size = 30)
```
:::

:::{.column width=45%}

```{r}
pancakes |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = treatment, 
             y = rating, 
             color = treatment)) + 
  geom_jitter(height = 0,
              width = .2,
              alpha = .7,
              size = 3) +
  labs(x = "treatment") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```



:::
:::




## Kruskal-Wallis Test - Procedure

1. Rank the responses from 1 to n
    - $y_{ij} \rightarrow r_{ij}$ 
2. Find the average rank within each treatment group
3. Find the overall average rank
4. Compute: $H = (n-1) \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^r (\bar{r}_{i\cdot}-  \bar{r}_{\cdot\cdot})^2}{\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^r (\bar{r}_{ij}-  \bar{r}_{\cdot\cdot})^2}$ 
5. Compare $H$ to $\chi_{(t-1)}^2$


## Kruskal-Wallis Test - in R




```{r}
#| echo: true

kruskal.test(rating ~ treatment, 
             data = pancakes)
```


:::columns

:::column
:::callout-warning
### Definitely correct to use the non-parametric test here


We could tell from the context that the outcome was not normally distributed... and the model diagnostics from the ANOVA would have confirmed, as shown to the right.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
#| eval: false

lm(rating ~ treatment, 
   pancakes) |> 
  broom::augment() |> 
  ggpubr::ggqqplot(x = ".resid",
         color = "#3a86d4") +
  labs(title = "Normal QQ-Plot of Residuals for Pancake Data with ANOVA model")
```

:::
:::

:::column

:::callout-warning
###  QQplot

```{r}
lm(rating ~ treatment, 
   pancakes) |> 
  broom::augment() |> 
  ggpubr::ggqqplot(x = ".resid",
         color = "#3a86d4") +
  labs(title = "Normal QQ-Plot of Residuals for Pancake Data with ANOVA model")
```
:::

:::

:::


## Friedman's Test (RCBD)

- Extension of Wilcoxon Ranked Sum for RCBDs
- Same idea with ranks!


1. Rank the responses **within blocks**
2. Find the average rank within each treatment group **across blocks**
3. Find the overall average rank
4. Compute test statistic $Q$, which compares the rank differences across treatments (very similar to $H$)
5. Compare $Q$ to $\chi_{(t-1)}^2$


## Friedman's Test -- Example

You realize that there is a lot of variability between raters for the pancakes. So you decide to re-do the study with just 12 of your friend, where each get a short stack made with each of the temperature & time combinations. You randomize the order, but making sure that each possible order occurs exactly 3 times.


```{r}
pancakes_blocked <- pancakes |> 
  arrange(treatment, rating) |> 
  group_by(treatment) |> 
  mutate(block = row_number())
```

```{r}
#| echo: true

friedman.test(rating ~ treatment | block,
              data = pancakes_blocked)
```



## Bootstrapping OR Randomization Tests

- All you need for inference...
  - A test statistic
  - A **null distribution** for the test statistic (i.e. what would typical values be of the test statistic, assuming $H_0$ is true?)
  
- Given a test statistic, bootstrapping and randomization inference get you a null distribution when you don't have theory to back you up

- More on randomization testing Thursday... you have actually seen a lot of these in STAT I & II at Cal Poly!
